# sitesolide

> sitesolide deploys small software, static sites and apps in any language, to one Debian server its owner runs: `sitesolide deploy` in a folder puts it live on HTTPS, restricted when private, open only to the people given access, with secrets held on the server: `sitesolide.json` names them, the server keeps the values, and only the owner reads one back. There is no staging: a real deploy is live for every visitor at once.

This file is for an agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) that uses the `sitesolide` CLI on a user's behalf. `sitesolide --help` prints every command; the links below are the reference.

**Every deployment goes through a token.** `sitesolide deploy` builds on this workstation and uploads the result to the dashboard's API, `https://dashboard.<zone>`, with a token, `sst_` then 43 characters; none goes over SSH, the owner's included. What an agent needs to deploy is this file, `SITESOLIDE_API=https://dashboard.<zone>` and `SITESOLIDE_TOKEN` in its environment, both together, and nothing else: no configuration, no SSH key, no server name. The user hands the token over without pasting it into the conversation: in the environment, which wins over the files, or `sitesolide login --url https://dashboard.<zone> --token-stdin` with the token piped in, which checks it and keeps it in `~/.config/sitesolide/secrets/team-token`, 0600, with the address beside it; the token `login` kept goes to that address alone, and a `SITESOLIDE_API` or a `config.json` naming another dashboard is refused `unauthenticated`: never point either elsewhere. Where a token comes from:

- the owner's own, for every project: `sitesolide login --owner` on the owner's workstation mints it over their SSH access, straight into the vault, never shown; or the Tokens page of the dashboard, New token, "Every project, as you". It deploys every project the server carries, creates any, opens a site to the public, declares a domain and `"network": "outbound"`, sets secrets, and alone carries `--force` and `--adopt`;
- a token of chosen projects, for an agent or a CI, which the owner creates on the Tokens page. Only the owner mints tokens. What its scope does not allow is refused `out-of-scope`: never work around it with another slug or token.

**Is it installed and set up?**

- `sitesolide --version --json` ends with a `result` carrying `version`. If the command is missing, the user installs it: `curl -fsSL https://github.com/cthiriet/sitesolide/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh` (one binary in `~/.local/bin`, no Bun needed). Without it, deploy with `deploy.sh` (below).
- `sitesolide status --json`, from any folder, says which mode the workstation is in and whether it works:
  - a `result` with `api`, `identity` and `projects`: a token, through the dashboard's API; `identity.scope.all` true is the owner's token for every project;
  - a `result` with `projects`, `ports` and `memory`: the owner's workstation, which also reaches the server over SSH for the owner's other commands; `sitesolide deploy` there still needs a token, and says how to mint one when it has none (`sitesolide login --owner`);
  - an `error` whose message starts `missing settings:`: nothing is configured and no token is in the environment. With a token, set `SITESOLIDE_API` and `SITESOLIDE_TOKEN`, or run `sitesolide login`. A new server is `machine` then `setup` (below); a server already installed is `sitesolide init --server <user@host> --zone <dns.zone> --email <address>`. Never guess a server, a zone or a dashboard's address;
  - any other `error`: follow its `hint`.
- The configuration is `~/.config/sitesolide/config.json` (`server`, `zone`, `email`; `api` with a token), or `$SITESOLIDE_CONFIG_DIR/config.json` for a second installation. The `secrets/` folder beside it holds the workstation's credentials: never read it.

**Deploying a folder.**

1. `sitesolide detect --json`: an `inferred` event, then a `result` with `kind`, `manifest`, `reasons`, `notes`, `written`. It reads no server and writes nothing. The `notes` name the secrets the code reads, which the manifest declares by name under `secrets`, and the network calls it makes.
2. Review the manifest and the notes with the user, who decides `"network": "outbound"` (without it a service reaches only the loopback, DNS included), what the code reads and where each value lives: `env` for what anyone may read (a public URL, a framework's public key), names under `secrets` for runtime values the server keeps in the project's store (`"secrets": ["API_KEY"]`), `secrets.files` for a file read whole at `$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/files_<name>`, `secrets.build` for a value the build alone needs, taken from whoever deploys (`"secrets": { "runtime": [...], "files": [...], "build": [...] }`), a value never written in the manifest; a service's `backup` command when it runs a server database in the data folder (PostgreSQL, MongoDB: the hourly snapshot refuses one without it), and the slug, which is the address `https://<slug>.<zone>/`. `sitesolide detect --write` writes `sitesolide.json`, never over an existing one; `--slug <name>` names the project otherwise than after its folder. Every key: docs/manifest.md.
3. `sitesolide deploy --dry-run --json`: the machine judges the manifest as a deployment would and plans it, writing nothing: the systemd units and the Caddy block it would lay come as `file` events, the ports it would choose and what it would do as `info` and `planned`, and a refusal (`out-of-scope`, `invalid-manifest`) comes back now rather than at the deploy. It does not run the build (`--build` does) and sends nothing but the manifest. Show the user what it plans.
4. Once the user agrees: `sitesolide deploy --json`. In a folder still without a manifest, `sitesolide deploy --yes --json` writes the inferred one and deploys; it is refused when the server already has a project of that name: pick another `--slug`, never deploy over it.
5. Read the last line. A `result` carries `slug`, `kind` (`static`, `service`, `services`), `port`, `url` and `status`, the HTTP status the address answers this workstation (null when it does not resolve here yet; the machine already verified it): give the user the `url`. Its `missingSecrets` (`runtime`, `files`) names what the server lacks: a missing runtime secret never stops a deploy; generate the random keys the project checks itself with `sitesolide secrets generate NAME --json`, and ask the user to set the others (below). `manifestWritten: true` means `sitesolide.json` changed on disk (an inferred manifest, a port chosen, general access set from the dashboard): commit it. An `error` carries a `hint`: follow it.
6. A failed restart, or a site answering 500 or 502: `sitesolide logs --json --lines 100`, one `log` event per entry with `at`, `unit`, `priority`, `message`; priority 3 and below are errors. Fix the code, deploy again.

An app without `port` gets the lowest free one from `deploy`, in 3000 to 3099 and then in 21000 to 29999 once those are taken, written back into `sitesolide.json`. A port taken: delete `port` and deploy again. A port of 21000 to 29999 is refused on a server that has not opened that block yet ("the server has not opened the second block of service ports", or `second-block-closed` with a token): only the owner opens it, never run the commands the refusal names; until then set a free port of 3000 to 3099, or tell the user.

**Background work.** `detect` infers web servers and static sites only; a process that is not one goes under `services`, by hand, never as the top-level `start`, which is always a server. A worker, `{ "start": "...", "internal": true }` with no `port`, runs for good, listens on nothing and is restarted with growing delays when it falls; it should exit cleanly on SIGTERM. A scheduled service, `{ "start": "...", "schedule": "*:0/15", "timeout": "15m" }`, runs to its end at the times a systemd calendar expression names (`hourly`, `daily`, `Mon..Fri 08:00`, `*-*-* 06:30 Europe/Paris`), `timeout` 1h by default and 24h at most, with no `port`, `routes` or `backup`; a deployment does not run it. `cpu` (`50%` is half a core) caps a service, or every one at the top level. A project of workers and scheduled services alone, without `publicDir`, serves no page: its address answers a line saying so, and `domain` is refused. `deploy` stops on a schedule systemd on the machine does not read, and fails when a server or worker falls within ten seconds of its restart: read `logs`. A headless browser, heavy computing and mass email from the machine's own address do not belong on the machine that serves every site: tell the user before writing one (docs/manifest.md, "What fits on the machine").

**The `--json` contract.** Every command but `init` and `run` takes `--json`. Standard output then carries one JSON object per line and nothing else, and the run ends with exactly one `result` (`ok: true`, `command`, the command's data) or one `error` (`message`, `details`, `hint`), always the last line; a failure exits non-zero. Before it: `step`, `info`, `planned` (`message`); `warning` (`message`, `details`), to relay to the user; `output` (`stream`, `line`), a line of the build, rsync or a script; `file` (`name`, `content`); `inferred`; `log`; `check` (`step`, `status` among `done`, `ok`, `skip`, `todo`, `fail`, `title`, `detail`), one line of setup's or upgrade's checklist. Under `--json` nothing prompts and ssh never asks: the key must be loaded (`ssh-add`) and the host key already known, or the connection fails at once. Every command's `result` fields: docs/agents.md.

**What changes something.** `sitesolide deploy` changes the live site unless `--dry-run`, `sitesolide share` with an address who may open the app and its data (over the owner's SSH), and `sitesolide secrets generate` a key on the server: keep them among the commands your client asks the user about, never allowed once and for all. `detect`, `status`, `logs`, `share` alone, `lock --status`, `secrets` and `deploy --dry-run` only read. `--force` and `--adopt` on a deploy, `remove`, `lock`, `unlock`, `domain --activate`, `setup`, `upgrade` and `refresh` stay the owner's decision (below).

**What a token runs.** `deploy` (`--dry-run`, `--build`, `--yes`, `--slug`, and for the owner's token `--force`, which replaces a unit or a block edited by hand on the machine, and `--adopt`, which takes a name back from the token that holds it first), `status`, `logs` (`--lines` up to 500), `secrets` and `restart` run through the dashboard, and `detect` as anywhere. `--force` or `--adopt` with any other token is refused `out-of-scope`. The owner's machine-wide commands (`lock`, `unlock`, `domain`, `remove`, `run`, `share`, `passkey`, `refresh`, `backups`) run over the owner's SSH and are refused with a token, `needs-ssh`. A new project of a token without the public permission is Restricted. After a deploy, `sitesolide.json` follows the server: the ports it chose, general access set from the dashboard and the former names a rename left are written back (`manifestWritten: true`): commit it.

**Without the CLI: deploy.sh.** [deploy.sh](deploy.sh) makes the same deployment with bash, curl, tar and a JSON reader (jq, node, bun or python3). With `SITESOLIDE_API` and `SITESOLIDE_TOKEN` exported:

1. `curl -fsSL https://github.com/cthiriet/sitesolide/releases/latest/download/deploy.sh -o ~/deploy.sh`, outside the project, or the archive carries it;
2. `bash ~/deploy.sh --dry-run` from the project's folder: the machine's plan, the manifest it would lay with its ports and door, nothing built nor sent but the manifest; show it to the user;
3. `bash ~/deploy.sh` on their yes: the manifest, judged first; the build here; the archive; the machine's log to the end. It exits 0 only once the machine says `succeeded`, and names the ports it chose, which you then write into `sitesolide.json` (`"port"` after `start`) and commit. `--force` as the CLI's, the owner's token alone; `--archive <file>` builds and writes the archive without sending it.

It needs a `sitesolide.json` (write one with `sitesolide detect --write`, or by hand from docs/manifest.md), reads build secrets from the environment alone, and reads no store: the machine's log names the runtime secrets missing. Its calls and the archive's format: docs/access.md, "The API, for an agent without the CLI".

**Secrets.** Values live on the server, in the project's store, and never come back out: no route hands one to a token, an agent, the build or SSH; only the owner reads one, in the unlocked dashboard. `sitesolide secrets --json` lists the names, each with whether the store holds it (`source`: `store` or `none`), the declared ones `missing`, the files read at `$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/files_<name>`, the build's names and whether a restart is pending, never a value; it runs over the owner's SSH, or with a token minted with Manage secrets (a token without it is refused `out-of-scope`), which sets, generates and removes any name of its project's store. `sitesolide secrets generate NAME --json` draws a random value on the server, never returned, for a key the project checks itself (a session secret, an internal token, a database password before its first use), never for a provider's key; a name already set is refused `already-present`, and replacing it is the user's decision. `sitesolide secrets set NAME` is for the user to run in their own terminal, typing the value at its prompt; an agent pipes to `sitesolide secrets set NAME --stdin --json` only a value it generated itself, never one read from the conversation, the repository or a message, and never `NAME=value` or a value as an argument, which is refused before anything is sent. A name that looks like a value, over 64 characters or starting like a service's key, is refused `looks-like-value`, never quoted: tell the user it may be in the shell's history and to change it at its source. `secrets remove NAME...` takes names out, `secrets set-file NAME < path` and `secrets remove-file NAME` handle a file, and `--restart` restarts the service after any change. A deploy never stops on a missing runtime secret: it warns and lists them in `missingSecrets`. A missing build secret stops it before anything is sent: tell the user to export it or add it to `~/.config/sitesolide/secrets/<slug>.env`, which an agent never reads. `unconfirmed` means a change was sent and no answer came: check with `sitesolide secrets --json`, then run the same command once more, never in a loop. `sitesolide restart --json`, which any token that deploys the project may run, restarts its service and ends in an `error` unless it holds: read `logs` then.

**Access.** A restricted site opens to the owner and the project's guests alone. A guest has password access: a password the machine draws, which opens that site and nothing more, no dashboard and no token. A token never gives anyone access.

- `sitesolide share --json`, over the owner's SSH, reads the general access (`public`, `restricted`, `code`) and the guests, `entries` (each `who`, `by`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `expiresAt`, `expired`).
- `sitesolide share alice@example.com --json` gives password access, `--expires 24h|7d|30d|never`, 7d by default; `--remove <email>` takes it away from their next request. The password comes back once, in the result's `changes` (each `who`, `change`: `add`, `none` or `remove`, and `password`), for the user to send. Never store or repeat it.
- Access gives real people the app and its data. Ask the user who should get in, give it to exactly the addresses they named and nobody else, tell them who will get in and wait for their yes.
- In the dashboard, a site's Access section shows the same, general access first, then its guests. It is the user's, not an agent's.
- Never make a site Public: general access is the dashboard's. With a token, `share` is refused `needs-ssh`.

**A new server.** Run these only when the user asked for a server; the tokens are theirs.

- `sitesolide machine create --provider <provider> --name <name> --json` orders a Debian 13 VM from `hetzner`, `digitalocean`, `aws`, `gcp`, `azure`, `vultr`, `linode` or `scaleway` (each provider's cheapest current type with 2 GB in Europe unless `--type`, `--location`) with a firewall opening 22, 80, 443 and ICMP and the workstation's SSH key, then waits until SSH lets its account in. The `result` carries `machine` and `next`, the `setup` command to run, which names the account the image lets in (`root`, or a sudoer such as AWS's `admin`, with `--user deploy`). `sitesolide machine providers --json` says which providers have credentials on this workstation and where they come from. Credentials come from the provider's environment variables, standard input with `--token-stdin`, or the provider's own CLI already signed in, never an option. `sitesolide machine list --provider <provider> --json` lists what sitesolide created. An interrupted run is finished by running the same command again. `sitesolide setup` alone at a terminal is an interactive wizard for a person: an agent never runs it bare, it runs `machine create` then `setup` with its options.
- `sitesolide setup root@<ipv4> --zone <dns.zone> --email <address> --json` hardens the machine, creates the DNS records through Cloudflare's API (`--dns cloudflare`, the default; `--dns manual` when the zone's DNS is anywhere else, the records made by hand and each name getting its own certificate; no other provider is spoken to), installs every component and writes the configuration. It is idempotent and resumable: on an installed machine it changes nothing, after a failure it resumes at the failed step. `--dry-run` checks every step and changes nothing. Cloudflare's token comes from `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` or standard input with `--cloudflare-token-stdin` (docs/dns/cloudflare.md); under `--json` it never prompts. It is laid on the machine for Caddy: it must be scoped to the zone, and an agent never reuses a token that reaches the whole account. A configuration naming another `dns`, a provider since removed, is refused: the machine keeps serving, and which of the two it moves to is the user's decision (docs/upgrading.md). A machine with no public address, behind a NAT at home or in a VM, is served through a Cloudflare Tunnel the user creates first with `cloudflared tunnel create`: `--tunnel ~/.cloudflared/<id>.json`, a file an agent passes by its path and never reads, prints nor copies, since it holds the tunnel's secret (docs/tunnel.md).
- The run that draws the dashboard's and the portal's passwords prints them once on standard error, for the user, never in an event: never repeat, store or use them.
- A configuration that names another server, zone or account stops setup; it may point at a machine in service. A second installation gets `--config-dir <dir>` on setup, then `SITESOLIDE_CONFIG_DIR=<dir>` before every command.
- `sitesolide upgrade --dry-run --json` reads the configured machine and lists every component the CLI's release would change, each `up-to-date`, `out-of-date` or `missing`, changing nothing. `sitesolide upgrade --json` redeploys only the components found out of date, live, so only when the user asked; it never installs a missing one (`setup` does, the `result` carries the command in `next`), never reads a secret, and resumes at the failed component when run again.
- `sitesolide refresh --all --dry-run --json` reads every project's manifest on the server and lists the units this release would write again, each project `outdated`, `current`, `kept` (a unit edited by hand, never replaced), `refused` or `static`, changing nothing. `sitesolide refresh --all --json` writes those units, without sending any code, and restarts and checks each project's services, live, one project at a time, stopping at the first that does not hold: only when the user asked, after an upgrade whose notes say the generated units changed. `refresh <slug>` does one project.

**Rules an agent never breaks.**

- Secret values never go into the repository, `sitesolide.json`, `env`, a command-line argument or the conversation: the manifest lists names alone. The user sets values in the dashboard's Secrets section, `https://dashboard.<zone>`, or runs `sitesolide secrets set NAME` themselves and types the value at its prompt; an agent draws random keys with `sitesolide secrets generate`, and pipes to `sitesolide secrets set NAME --stdin` only a value it generated itself, never one from the conversation. A deploy missing a runtime secret goes on and lists it in `missingSecrets`: tell the user, who sets it, then restart. Never read, print or guess a secret, nor ask the user to paste one. Tokens, a cloud provider's, Cloudflare's or a sitesolide token, reach the CLI through environment variables or standard input only.
- Never change the server by hand: no `ssh`, `sudo`, `systemctl` or file edits there; everything goes through the CLI. Never `caddy stop` or `caddy start`: they talk to the Caddy in service whatever `--config` says, and a stop takes every site down.
- Only on the user's explicit decision, never on your own: `upgrade` and `refresh` (their `--dry-run` only reads), `--force` over a file edited on the machine, `--adopt` over a name another token holds, minting a token (`sitesolide login --owner`), `setup --dns-replace` over records that point elsewhere, `setup --any-os`, `machine destroy --confirm <name>` (the disk and the provider's backups go with it), `remove --confirm <slug>` (what changed since the last backup is lost), `lock`, `unlock`, `domain --activate` or `--deactivate`, and giving access to anyone the user did not name.
- Every `error` carries a `hint`: follow it, and never answer a refusal with `--force` or a workaround. A refused or dropped SSH connection during setup is most likely a fail2ban ban of this workstation: never retry in a loop; wait the 10 minutes it lasts, then run the same command once.
- Never run `sitesolide passkey link` nor `sitesolide passkey remove`, and never unlock the dashboard: the link signs in as the owner for fifteen minutes, so the user runs it in their own terminal and opens it in their own browser. The owner signs in to the dashboard with a passkey, and once one exists the dashboard's password no longer signs in.
- What is deployed is live at once: dry-run first, show the user, and deploy on their yes.

## Docs

- [Agents](docs/agents.md): the `--json` events and every command's `result`, zero configuration, the skill
- [Commands](docs/commands.md): everything the CLI does, with a token and over the owner's SSH
- [The manifest](docs/manifest.md): every key of sitesolide.json and what it changes
- [Access and tokens](docs/access.md): who may open a site, the owner's passkeys, login and the owner's token, what a token may deploy, the control API and its error codes
- [Secrets](docs/secrets.md): `env`, the server's store, files at `$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/files_<name>`, build secrets with whoever deploys, and why never in git
- [Setup](docs/setup.md): every step of `sitesolide setup`, what it refuses, the token and the passwords
- [Behind a tunnel](docs/tunnel.md): `setup --tunnel`, a machine with no public address served through a Cloudflare Tunnel, and what it cannot carry
- [A machine from a cloud provider](docs/machine.md): `sitesolide machine create`, `list`, `destroy` and `providers`, and the credentials they need, with a page per cloud in docs/providers/
